entry.title: Where do we want this story to go?

link.title: Where do we want this story to go?

entry.content:
My research is focused on an animal species that I never thought I would study: humans.

Specifically my research is focused on human communication. Or, even more specifically, on how we can take a more strategic approach to communications in order to encourage greater public engagement and behaviour change for biodiversity conservation.

It's a seemingly obscure topic.

But it's strangely topical right now, because the importance of clear, effective communication is rarely higher than during a global health crisis.

I recently made a post to my research lab's blog, giving some advice to conservation professionals (whoever that is...is that what I am?) about how to talk about COVID-19. In it, I discuss the important of generosity and understanding, accuracy, being clear on the purpose of communications, and being careful with use of language. These elements of communication are always important, but in a crisis situation they become critical.

I ended the piece asking myself a question:

Where do we want this story to go?

"Looking long term, it now seems undeniable that coronavirus is changing the world, and the social context in which we continue to research and work will be different even if we eventually return 'back to normal'. 

As conservation scientists we don't want to see COVID-19 create a new social and narrative context where taking action on issues like biodiversity conservation or climate change are even more difficult. As communicators, we need to think about where we want the story to go. Perhaps economic reform as a result of COVID-19 could also make progress towards a more sustainable future? Perhaps rather than bouncing back, we can bounce forward after coronavirus?"

Coronavirus is changing the world, and the new stories that emerge from these changes will set the stage for where we go next. And we all have the power to create and share these new stories.

"We can start to lay the foundation for these conversations now by avoiding comparing crises (e.g. by lamenting that biodiversity conservation hasn’t had the same response as COVID-19) and focus instead on needing kindness and cooperation, and scientific expertise. Some current responses to COVID-19 convey border control and security message frames, which don’t set a healthy narrative context for action for biodiversity conservation or climate change."

We need to avoid the stories that pull us back to where we were, and focus on the stories that push us towards where we want to be.

"By focusing instead on humanity’s ability to band together in the face of an existential crisis, and asking people to continue to have courage, we allow the space for future calls for action to tackle climate change. By highlighting that we have been able to make changes to our way of life when called for, we increase public perceptions of our collective impact and strengthen our own self-belief that we can make meaningful change.

In doing this we foster a narrative of cooperation amidst a crisis, where we listen to the advice of experts, and are able to find solutions to complex and global problems, setting the stage for progress towards a more sustainable future."

Because stories are important. They make things possible. They set the frame for our future.

Let's make it a good one.

You can find the full blog post, How to talk about COVID-19 for conservation professionals, on the ICON Science website here.

entry.title: A Selection of Pages from 2019
entry.content:
I started 2019 reading in a cabin on the beach in Simon’s Town, South Africa. I was reading outside on a deck staring out onto False Bay, a towel across my lap, sunscreen haphazardly slathered on my arms and legs, and a cap on my head. Sea air refreshing my lungs and skin from two weeks of camping in Kenya and Uganda. Thanks to the haphazard sunscreen slathering, my legs and neck were gradually turning red in strange patches throughout the day, until I retreated to the couch inside, covered in red rugs and woven cushions. Not a bad start to the year, all things considered.

In that cabin, I felt worlds away from the slums we’d passed on the drive out of Cape Town’s city centre. Simon’s Town – named after the first governor (a Dutch colonist) – felt closer to my parent’s beach house on the Victorian coastline (or the writing retreat of an aspiring upper-middle class poet), than the African savannahs I had pictured when planning my trip. This place was another continent and yet strikingly similar to home. Our trek up Table Mountain and through the Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden had been a tour of Acacia plants, whose sister’s reside in Australia. Kenya and Uganda had been filled with introduced Eucalyptus trees. I picked out two books from the cabin’s bookshelves to start my year of reading. 

First up Table Mountain: To Cape Point by Carrie Hampton. Full of beautiful pictures and information about the area. It could have been a Great Ocean Road souvenir book – a reminder of the super familiar yet different atmosphere I felt in Africa, particularly South Africa. The book didn’t feel foreign or different at all. As a white tourist, in group of white women, the strangeness of South Africa was easy to momentarily overlook. It was easy for it to look like home from different angles, from the pretty coastal landscape angles to the ugly colonial segregated (white) world-undermining angles. It was yet another colonial wake-up call. A reminder that colonisation is ongoing there and ongoing back home and I am part of it, whether I choose to see it or not and wherever on earth I am.

Next off the cabin’s shelf was Gift from the Sea by Anne Morrow Lindbergh. I can’t remember what this book was about, but it was familiar. The cut and language and smell of it reeked of childhood and books passed to me by honorary aunts and family friends. The pages were browning on the edges and the blue cover seemed imbued with sea salt. I devoured it quickly, like any human or seagull devours hot chips on the beach. GoodReads advises that it is one of those books offering musings and meanderings on life, so it makes sense I devoured it quickly in the context of a New Year and yet don’t remember any of the pieces of advice it offered.

Throughout my trip to Africa I had attempted to reread The Metamorphosis and Other Stories by Franz Kafka. It had the bonus of being a translated work that instantly put me ahead for Book Bingo for 2019 (yes, I have a Book Bingo for the year, shush you). I had read The Metamorphosis before, but Kafka’s shorter stories offered fragments of social commentary that felt meaningful and timely to start a year of personal and political change. Still, not that easy to read. I finished it back home rotating between my bed, my garden lined with jasmine flowers and the lounge room lined with a million cushions.

From there I also read The Old Man and the Sea by Ernest Hemingway. A classic that’s been sitting on my bookshelf for a while and I had never read. It seems it’s my curse to be forever disappointed by the classics. I enjoy the language and the insight to everyday life they offer, but otherwise my 21st century plot-focused mind is forever waiting for the twist or conflict or world-shattering reveal in the final moments. Perhaps Game of Thrones has forever ruined slice of life content for me, or I should pre-read synopses to know what I’m in for before I hang out for twists when the book is simply about an old man and the sea (and musings on life and death and meaning etc.).

At Clunes Book Festival 2019 (one of my favourite places and events in the entire world) I purchased upwards of 17 books, including two copies of Aviary Wonders Inc. Spring Catalog and Instruction Manual by Kate Samworth. A satirical, beautiful, heart-wrenching, existential piece of art that you definitely shouldn’t gift to anyone, because anyone who would appreciate this book will find it completely depressing and everyone else just won’t get it. But you should. Get it, I mean. The book imagines a scenario where all birds are extinct and offers a catalogue for designing your own perfect bird. Out of all the books I’ve read this book summarises 2019 best for me, which is rather depressing. The past few years has seen the state of the climate discussed somewhat more productively in the media. The School Strikes have done much to mainstream calls for action, there is a gradual shift from a focus on individual behaviours to systemic changes needed, and the Australian Conservation Foundation (alongside other media, non-for-profit and political groups) weren’t wrong when they labelled the Australian Federal Election the 'climate election'. Yet the outcome of that election was rotten for the environment, the current Australian government is currently working on tearing down so-called “green tape” (which, to be frank, is already as weak as ‘tape’ sounds), and it looks like hardly any country is going to meet their climate targets.

In times like this, it sometimes feels immensely privileged of me to be focused on issues of biodiversity conservation and extinction rather than climate change or other social issues. Yet these issues are inherently linked, and our biggest problems involve both of them. The drying up of the Murray Darling is bad for water and bad for fish biodiversity. We lose species (i.e. biodiversity), we lose important functions of ecosystems, ecosystems that we have already altered beyond recognition. We still don’t quite understand the repercussions of all this, but I’ll let you in on a little secret: it ain’t good. I don’t think it’s useful to discuss my existential/apocalyptic fears too much here, but I think it’s important to consider (especially given recent events) that the changing climate is already impacting people around the world. Even if those people aren’t us or our loved ones yet, I reckon we should start to do something to create a better future for all of us.

But let’s push aside those dark thoughts for today and turn to nicer things, like book recommendations from friends! This year I was recommended The Lagoon: How Aristotle Invented Science by Armand Marie Leroi. This book took me way too long to read. My excuse is that while it was beautifully written, it was dense and difficult for me to read after a day PhD-ing. Recommend to science writing and philosophy of science nerds. It is truly beautiful and fascinating, but requires some energy. I was also recommended The Village Effect: Why Face-to-Face Contact is Good for Our Health, Happiness, Learning, and Longevity by Susan Pinker. This book feels like a long-form The Guardian or The Conversation science article, and I don’t know whether that’s a good or bad thing. I think it’s a good thing because it’s easy to read and packed full of interesting information. I think it’s a bad thing because I feel like I quickly scrolled/scanned through and only learnt what I already knew and/or believed to be true. Basically having friends and a partner is good unless you get fooled by an identity thief. But yeah, self-care / socialising is important for everyone, we’re social animals go figure. (In hindsight, I appreciate that the friend/s recommending this to me were probably trying to subtly tackle my PhD stress.)

After years of slowly chipping away on holidays, in courtyards and in the aforementioned cushion-infested lounge room I finally finished Alan Turing: The Enigma by Andrew Hodges. I honestly think this book is written very well considering its content and dutiful focus on the mathematical research of Alan Turing. However, it was incredibly difficult for me to read after a day at the office, and, honestly, maybe I just don’t care enough about maths (gasp!). Alan Turing’s story is fascinating, horrible and important, but the interesting parts weren’t enough for me to muster up the focus needed to comprehend the detail of his work. My favourite parts were when the author discussed in simpler language the importance of Turing’s work, as well as the final chapters when he discussed in detail the social context and attitudes around homosexuality in his final years as well as the years preceding. Highly recommend to maths/computer/engineering-focused friends. But otherwise, just read some Wikipedia pages and save yourself a year or two.

Thanks to my own reluctance to give up on some of the more challenging reads discussed above (as well as my own distraction by other important facets of life…), I didn’t meet my reading goal for this year. I definitely didn’t read enough to write a post with my favourite books of the year, let alone my favourite science or natural history writing. But so be it. I’m ending the year in my adorably shaky share house, reading some delightfully distracting fiction, being talked into playing video games by my housemates, and getting excited for a busy, challenging, climate-tackling 2020. Come at me.

entry.title: Chasing Mr Toad
entry.content:
If there was a time in my life when I was absolutely dripping in sweat, then this was it.

There were beads of the stuff all over my face, and I was leaning into a blast of musty air con, only moving away to gulp down some electrolytes. I suppose that may sound like hell, but honestly, I was having the time of my life.

Welcome to fieldwork.

I was taking shelter in a dusty 4WD on a cattle station, sitting on the coast between Broome and Port Hedland in Western Australia. More importantly, I was chasing down a rather infamous Australian pest: the Cane Toad (Rhinella marina).

[caption id="attachment_82" align="alignnone" width="3888"] ...and here we have Mr Toad wearing a stunning ball chain belt complete with radio transmitter. Photo: R Hayes[/caption]

While us ecologists are usually keen on keeping our study species around, I was wishing this particular Mr Toad would go back to South America, and leave our poor native predators alone. Unfortunately, that ship sailed in 1935, and over the past 80 years the toad has thrived in our landscape.

With no natural predators, the toad is free to breed more efficiently than rabbits, and spread wherever the climate permits it. Any native animal attempting to take a bite of a toad at best end up reviling at the taste, and at worst are taken out by the toad’s toxin, resulting in species declines. The toad is now established in the north of Western Australia, and is expected to continue moving south-west towards the Pilbara, in the south of Western Australia.

This is what brought me to a cattle station in the middle of Western Australia.

The station sits within the so-called Kimberley-Pilbara corridor, an area which should be inhospitable to toads during the dry season, when all the natural water dries up. But this is cattle country, and so there are man-made water sources everywhere. And many of them leak.

[caption id="attachment_85" align="alignnone" width="3888"] Leaking pastoral tanks can result in massive pools of cane toad happy-places. Photo: R Hayes[/caption]

Previous computer simulations had predicted that by effectively removing these water sources (by upgrading infrastructure and preventing leaks), a barrier would be created, preventing toads from moving southwards towards the Pilbara.

But this idea needed on-ground testing. Enter me: a bright-eyed master’s student, keen for a challenging field project.

After half a year of writing and reviewing grant applications, ethics proposals and Park’s permits, I flew to Kununurra in Western Australia to collect 20 male toads and drive them down south to a cattle station within the barrier area.

Yes, I was moving a non-native animal into new territory; a horrible idea in most ecological circles. But these toads were all males (to prevent any breeding), and we were releasing them in a remote area far away from available water sources. More importantly, the toads were going to be radio-tracked intensively as part of my study, so the risk of establishment was ultimately minimal.

The waterless barrier strategy assumes that toads will be able to survive within the corridor during the wet season with no issues. During the dry, however, artificial water points (i.e. dams and tanks) should be the only water available to toads, meaning their removal will prevent their survival and create a barrier. The barrier simply needs to be wide enough to account for toad dispersal through the unrestrictive wet season.

But there were a few untested assumptions around previous work. Were we sure toads couldn’t survive here without those artificial water sources? What about shelter sites, such as goanna burrows? What about coastal fogs providing moisture through morning dew?

To answer these questions, I started by attaching a radio transmitter to each toad by measuring out little belts made from a ball chain and clipping them around the toads’ waists. They were released at night into the desert, far away from any artificial water sources.

[caption id="attachment_87" align="alignnone" width="3888"] A gorgeous landscape to be working in. Absolutely filled with ankle-twisting and toad-sheltering goanna burrows. Photo: R Hayes[/caption]

The following morning myself and a research volunteer rose early and went out to catch up with the toads. Waving an antenna around like madmen, we listened desperately for the tell-tale BEEP leading us to a sheltering toad.

One of the ways toads have adapted to the Australian landscape is through being active at night and sheltering during the day. In doing this they avoid the worst of the heat, reduce their water loss, and increase their survival ability.

We were therefore expecting the toads to shelter during the day, allowing us to determine which shelter sites they were selecting within the landscape. For the most part, they did (60% of the time, in fact), however, we found one headstrong individual not only not sheltering, but hopping along during the heat of the day!

Indeed, even sheltering toads moved substantial distances overnight, far above the distances we expected. One avid sprinter managed to move over 2.5 km in one night!

It's unsurprising then that occasionally a BEEP could not be found, and we had no choice but to trudge through the desert in 500 m blocks, heading up to 3 km away from our starting point, all in search of one singular spirited cane toad and the valuable data he represented. Never have I desired a dune buggy more.

Even once we tracked the BEEP to its source, finding the toads was not always easy. The toads were brilliant at finding shelter sites within the landscape, and within this landscape the majority of shelter sites were goanna burrows.

This meant that we often had to stick an inspection camera down the burrows to confirm exactly where the toads were. This also helped us to avoid sticking our hands down into potential snake territory...

 

[caption id="attachment_336" align="alignnone" width="2128"] Goanna burrows at two different study sites: the desert and coastal habitats. One of these is better shelter than the other...[/caption]

Once we finally found our toad, I weighed them to approximate their water loss, and recorded their GPS coordinates and shelter site type, such as a goanna burrow or shrub.

As part of our ethics requirements, we planned to humanely euthanise toads once they had lost 40% of their body weight (toads can survive losing 50%). Unfortunately, due to their unexpected speediness (and the harshness of the corridor environment), we were unable to locate many toads before they reached critical dehydration.

While an undoubtedly grim experience for the toads (and an emotional and philosophical trial for their human followers), this short survival time is ultimately a positive outcome for the waterless barrier strategy.

[caption id="" align="aligncenter" width="2128"] Plots showing survival (i.e., proportion of individuals alive) over time. (a) Overall survival. Dashed lines indicate 95% confidence intervals. (b) Effect of habitat on survival. * indicates censored points where a lost toad was last seen alive[/caption]

Most toads only survived 1-2 days, and our analysis predicts a maximum survival time of 5 days in this environment, supporting the assumption that toads cannot survive in this area without access to artificial water sources.

In the end, this project indicates that the waterless barrier is a feasible means to halt cane toad movement down the west Australian coast. This relatively inexpensive strategy could therefore be an effective way to protect species in the Pilbara from the toad's impact.

For my part, this project was my first taste of real field work and my first experience within Australia's vast semi-arid and arid environments, which I've since fallen in love with. If you're someone who has never left the eastern coast I absolutely insist you go out and explore more of this exceptional country.

I myself can't wait to get back out there.

Simple study question: Can cane toads survive in a potential barrier area without access to artificial water bodies during the dry season?

Simple study answer: No. The model predicts a maximum survival of 5 days in this environment. (Gregg et al. 2019).

Importance: Supports the waterless barrier strategy, allaying fears that toads would be able to survive in the barrier despite the removal of artificial water bodies.

In a word: Barrier

The toad is now established in the north of Western Australia, and is expected to continue moving south-west towards the Pilbara, in the south of Western Australia. This is what brought me to a cattle station in the middle of Western Australia. The station sits within the so-called Kimberley-Pilbara corridor, an area which should be inhospitable to toads during the dry season, when all the natural water dries up. But this is cattle country, and so there are man-made water sources everywhere. And many of them leak. [caption id="attachment_85" align="alignnone" width="3888"] Leaking pastoral tanks can result in massive pools of cane toad happy-places. Photo: R Hayes[/caption] Previous computer simulations had predicted that by effectively removing these water sources (by upgrading infrastructure and preventing leaks), a barrier would be created, preventing toads from moving southwards towards the Pilbara. But this idea needed on-ground testing. Enter me: a bright-eyed master’s student, keen for a challenging field project. After half a year of writing and reviewing grant applications, ethics proposals and Park’s permits, I flew to Kununurra in Western Australia to collect 20 male toads and drive them down south to a cattle station within the barrier area. Yes, I was moving a non-native animal into new territory; a horrible idea in most ecological circles. But these toads were all males (to prevent any breeding), and we were releasing them in a remote area far away from available water sources. More importantly, the toads were going to be radio-tracked intensively as part of my study, so the risk of establishment was ultimately minimal. The waterless barrier strategy assumes that toads will be able to survive within the corridor during the wet season with no issues. During the dry, however, artificial water points (i.e. dams and tanks) should be the only water available to toads, meaning their removal will prevent their survival and create a barrier. The barrier simply needs to be wide enough to account for toad dispersal through the unrestrictive wet season. But there were a few untested assumptions around previous work. Were we sure toads couldn’t survive here without those artificial water sources? What about shelter sites, such as goanna burrows? What about coastal fogs providing moisture through morning dew? To answer these questions, I started by attaching a radio transmitter to each toad by measuring out little belts made from a ball chain and clipping them around the toads’ waists. They were released at night into the desert, far away from any artificial water sources. [caption id="attachment_87" align="alignnone" width="3888"] A gorgeous landscape to be working in. Absolutely filled with ankle-twisting and toad-sheltering goanna burrows. Photo: R Hayes[/caption] The following morning myself and a research volunteer rose early and went out to catch up with the toads. Waving an antenna around like madmen, we listened desperately for the tell-tale BEEP leading us to a sheltering toad. One of the ways toads have adapted to the Australian landscape is through being active at night and sheltering during the day. In doing this they avoid the worst of the heat, reduce their water loss, and increase their survival ability. We were therefore expecting the toads to shelter during the day, allowing us to determine which shelter sites they were selecting within the landscape. For the most part, they did (60% of the time, in fact), however, we found one headstrong individual not only not sheltering, but hopping along during the heat of the day! Indeed, even sheltering toads moved substantial distances overnight, far above the distances we expected. One avid sprinter managed to move over 2.5 km in one night! It's unsurprising then that occasionally a BEEP could not be found, and we had no choice but to trudge through the desert in 500 m blocks, heading up to 3 km away from our starting point, all in search of one singular spirited cane toad and the valuable data he represented. Never have I desired a dune buggy more. Even once we tracked the BEEP to its source, finding the toads was not always easy. The toads were brilliant at finding shelter sites within the landscape, and within this landscape the majority of shelter sites were goanna burrows. This meant that we often had to stick an inspection camera down the burrows to confirm exactly where the toads were. This also helped us to avoid sticking our hands down into potential snake territory... [caption id="attachment_336" align="alignnone" width="2128"] Goanna burrows at two different study sites: the desert and coastal habitats. One of these is better shelter than the other...[/caption] Once we finally found our toad, I weighed them to approximate their water loss, and recorded their GPS coordinates and shelter site type, such as a goanna burrow or shrub. As part of our ethics requirements, we planned to humanely euthanise toads once they had lost 40% of their body weight (toads can survive losing 50%). Unfortunately, due to their unexpected speediness (and the harshness of the corridor environment), we were unable to locate many toads before they reached critical dehydration. While an undoubtedly grim experience for the toads (and an emotional and philosophical trial for their human followers), this short survival time is ultimately a positive outcome for the waterless barrier strategy. [caption id="" align="aligncenter" width="2128"] Plots showing survival (i.e., proportion of individuals alive) over time. (a) Overall survival. Dashed lines indicate 95% confidence intervals. (b) Effect of habitat on survival. * indicates censored points where a lost toad was last seen alive[/caption] Most toads only survived 1-2 days, and our analysis predicts a maximum survival time of 5 days in this environment, supporting the assumption that toads cannot survive in this area without access to artificial water sources. In the end, this project indicates that the waterless barrier is a feasible means to halt cane toad movement down the west Australian coast. This relatively inexpensive strategy could therefore be an effective way to protect species in the Pilbara from the toad's impact. For my part, this project was my first taste of real field work and my first experience within Australia's vast semi-arid and arid environments, which I've since fallen in love with. If you're someone who has never left the eastern coast I absolutely insist you go out and explore more of this exceptional country. I myself can't wait to get back out there. Simple study question: Can cane toads survive in a potential barrier area without access to artificial water bodies during the dry season? Simple study answer: No. The model predicts a maximum survival of 5 days in this environment. (Gregg et al. 2019). Importance: Supports the waterless barrier strategy, allaying fears that toads would be able to survive in the barrier despite the removal of artificial water bodies. In a word: Barrier

entry.title: When in doubt, go to the library

link.title: When in doubt, go to the library

entry.content:
Need some holiday reading? Gift ideas? Just want an excuse to buy some vaguely work-related novels and knock off early?

I've got you covered.

I've managed to read a few stellar books this year, many of which focus around the environment or natural history in one way or another, and all of which I highly recommend (to the right audience of course). So read on for my bookish recommendations in no particular order!

1. The Tapir's Morning Bath: Mysteries of the tropical rain forest and the scientists who are trying to solve them, Elizabeth Royte

For conservation scientists, ecologists, researchers (particularly students), and anyone wanting an inside look into their world

Okay, I'm cheating right off the bat because I did not read this book this year (although I've been known to leaf through and reread sections on bad days). However, I think it's worth a mention because this book is one of my absolute favourites and a major inspiration for this blog.

It centres around Barro Colorado Island in the middle of the Panama Canal, where our journalist writer follows around a force of scientists who are each trying to understand their own little part of the isolated rain forest. From monkey dung to philosophical meanderings on the goals of conservation science itself, this book has it all. The (real-life) characters are a joy to meet, and their academic / career struggles and fears will no doubt feel familiar to any student or wannabe academic.

2. Defending Biodiversity: Environmental Science and Ethics, Jonathan A. Newman

For academics, philosophers, debaters, and anyone interested in environmental issues

This was the first book I read in 2018, and while it felt like reading a textbook at times (welcome to academic texts), it was overall very illuminating. The book outlines and assesses major arguments for conserving biodiversity, considering both the instrumental (e.g. ecosystem services) or intrinsic (e.g. natural beauty) value of nature.

I would expect only the most dedicated to read this from top to tail – I myself was mainly  motivated by the need to write this book review – but I would genuinely recommend it for anyone interested in rethinking or interrogating their own ethics and arguments around biodiversity conservation, or indeed environmental issues in general. It's sure to add an edge to your future arguments.

3. Hidden Museum: A Cabinet of Curiosities, Shaun Parr

For curiosity seekers and short attention spans

This book here is at the entire other end of the spectrum when it comes to length and density. A borderline coffee table book, with very little text, this one is aptly named. It is simply a small collection of curiosities, focused around natural history. It also comes with a little red 'magnifying glass' so you can explore the pages yourself. I’ll say no more.

4. Hidden Nature: A Voyage of Discovery, Alys Fowler

For those in need of a holiday

I bought this book because of its beautiful cover and because I needed a break. This book provided exactly that. A perfect, breezy holiday read. You basically get to spend the entire book exploring Birmingham's canal network via kayak and watching the writer's garden grow (alongside an emotional internal journey).

This is a well-written book, but not a page-turner and certainly not action packed. In other words, give it to your "gardening gran" friend, not your "let's watch Mad Max: Fury Road again" friend.

5. The Sound of a Wild Snail Eating, Elisabeth Tova Bailey

For people who enjoy watching ants in the garden

Like Hidden Nature this one is a delightful, peaceful, and beautifully written book. However rather than a broad focus on canal environments, this little book focuses on a little subject: snails.

The bed-ridden narrator focuses our chaotic minds on the life of one small snail. She manages to drift in and out of snail physiology and evolution without breaking the captivating tone of the book. Great for a weekend read in your garden, or a mental health day in bed.

6. Dark Emu, Bruce Pascoe

For Australians

Recommended to me by many, I finally managed to cross this book off my “to-read” list. An absolutely fascinating (and worldview-shaking) look at the lives of precolonial Aboriginal Australians, particularly focused on their land use and management.

This book is jam-packed with evidence sourced primarily from early Australian colonial explorers, alongside frank and open language making it a particularly compelling and engaging read. Highly recommend to all.

Happy reading!

entry.title: Seeds in the Sand
entry.content:
I may be a little biased, but I find the Australian semi-arid landscape simply stunning.

What appears to be a desolate place on the surface suddenly bursts to life once you simply kneel down to the ground and take a proper look.

Down there you can see tracks left by bettongs hurtling through the sand the night before. You can see bustling rodent highways, trails left by an innumerable number of tiny rodent feet, lining the dunes. You can see seedlings sprouting from piles of sand excavated by bilbies. And after rain, you can see ancient shield shrimp scuttling around shallow, muddy puddles.

[caption id="attachment_307" align="aligncenter" width="3996"] A smattering of tracks at the Arid Recovery reserve, including one of my favourites: the Shingleback / Sleepy / Stumpy-tail Lizard's tracks.[/caption]

But while the arid landscape is littered with signs of diverse animal life, the plant life is similarly spectacular. The red sand and gibber plains which overwhelm the horizon are contrasted by plains of saltbush, shiny leaves of hopbush, and the grey-blue stillness of mulga trees.  And after a burst of rain the sudden addition of bright green vegetation is striking against the red sand.

So while many zoologists (we’re all friends here) sigh audibly at the mere mention of vegetation surveys, they simply don’t feel tiresome out here. And in any case, there’s something rather relaxing and peaceful about vegetation surveys.

They’re methodical and relatively quiet. There’s no animal handling stress (from either party, to our knowledge), no quick processing of a reluctant strong-kicking marsupial, and no peanut-allergy-inducing baits to put my confused immune system on red alert.

Perhaps most exciting is that vegetation surveys allow us to explore species which are so incredibly different from ourselves, species which can tower over us and spread their roots beneath our feet. Just take a moment, zoologists, and admit it (even if just to yourself): plants are pretty damn cool.

[caption id="attachment_308" align="aligncenter" width="3996"] The striking arid vegetation, and some evidence of herbivory...[/caption]

So there I was, out in the field again, wedging two pieces of a deconstructed ice-cream container into the ground and taking a sizeable sample of sand using a spoon as a shovel. Ecologists are nothing if not resourceful.

I imagine me carting giant snap-lock bags filled with sand across each dune made it appear as though I desperately wanted to take the entire desert home with me. But I was actually collecting a seed bank for PhD candidate, Charlotte Mills, who at that point was walking around with a giant square made out of piping, sampling plant species within quadrats (hence the giant square made out of piping).

Charlotte had set up exclusion pens throughout the Arid Recovery reserve, in order to investigate the pressure that the reintroduced herbivores were putting on the plants. By comparing between exclusion pens, which controlled which animals were allowed in, Charlotte was able to determine to what extent certain animals, such as the reintroduced Burrowing Bettong, Plains Mouse, and Hopping Mouse, were having an effect on the vegetation.

[caption id="attachment_315" align="aligncenter" width="3264"] The exclusion pens from above... Images: Charlotte Mills[/caption]

By having many sites set up on many dunes inside the Arid Recovery reserve, Charlotte ensured her results would be applicable across a broad landscape. She also carried out similar work in the Strzelecki desert, to consider how different communities of animals can drive differences in the vegetation. Within the Arid Recovery reserve Charlotte had 10 sites to monitor.

On the ground, this meant we had a lot of work to do. For each site we had to:

  1. Walk transects for tracks and scats to determine the animal community within each fenced site i.e. which animals and how many?
  2. Randomly sample the plant community through quadrat sampling (enter giant square made out of piping)
  3. Check up on the growth and health state of larger shrubs and trees

Those were the basics that Charlotte was monitoring every field trip as the centre of her research. Basics that would hopefully answer the question: what impact do herbivores (plant-eaters) and granivores (seed-eaters) have on vegetation communities?

But as researchers, we’re curious. And no matter how focused we are on a central question, others always crop up. This happens fairly often out in the field, where there’s always some element we haven’t considered. The trick is to notice the relevant ones.

Charlotte had noticed two.

What if the animals were ruining the chance of plants growing from the very beginning? What if they were eating the seeds hiding beneath the sand, seeds still waiting to germinate?

Cut to me on my knees, sampling dirt (or rather, a seed bank!) with a spoon. By looking closely at the seed bank, Charlotte could see if the bettongs and mice were changing which plants might have the opportunity to grow, and whether any were being eaten out of house and home!

Charlotte had also noticed that there was so much soil turnover at some of the incredibly active sites, which were absolutely littered with a mess of bettong tracks, that she tended to see less spider holes around. Out in this desert environment, spiders live in neat, impressive little holes and they’re a fairly common sight among the dunes. Could the mass of bettongs be messing with the spider’s ability to maintain reliable hidey holes?

We needed some data on this. So Charlotte decided to start counting spider holes as part of the tracks and scats transect.

[caption id="attachment_310" align="aligncenter" width="3996"] Fun Fact! Spider holes are incredibly hard for a non-expert with an iPhone camera to capture in focus...[/caption]

I happily completed the spider hole counting for a time. There are so many different kinds of spider (or ‘spidey’ for the professional ecologist) holes and they’re all damn fascinating. Some are made by the famous trapdoor spiders, but even those kinds vary from neat little flaps to giant openings disguised with leaf litter and grass.

Some are edged with vegetation that appears woven together forming gorgeous patterns around the dig. Others are so small that I could only determine it was a spider hole by peering in and spotting a scrunched up bunch of minute, hairy legs. All of these digs were so incredibly perfect: perfectly circular, perfectly smooth inside. They looked human-made, mechanically made. Spiders are truly incredible engineers.

There were a few moments, however, when my fascination was overshadowed by a primal fear of our eight-legged friends. Once in particular, I gazed around the exclusion pen, scanning the immense number of spider burrows around me, one after the other. I glanced down at the inordinately large tally on my notepad, and realised I was in a city of spiders. Well and truly surrounded.

While I set about dreamily peering into tiny burrows and musing over spider populations, Charlotte was set on truly investigating this question from as many angles as possible.

[caption id="attachment_312" align="aligncenter" width="3264"] Drone photos of the red sand. You can even spot animal tracks from this height! Images: Charlotte Mills[/caption]

Before we started trampling across each site – and carting away mounds of soil – Charlotte mustered the latest in human technology and took aerial photographs using a drone. These photographs allowed Charlotte to step away from the precise details we were collecting and visualise at a broad level the differences between her different fence treatments.

(Charlotte tells me she has since adorned her supervisor’s external office walls with drone pictures of red sand, shrubs and fences).

The Australian landscape has borne witness to some dramatic changes in its time. Since western colonisation invasive rabbits have had a dramatic effect on vegetation, and many of our native mammals have been pushed out, leaving us with little understanding of what makes a healthy, functioning ecosystem.

As a result, we can’t always be sure what is needed to properly ‘rewild’ damaged areas. Charlotte’s field work alone has already highlighted gaps in our knowledge, and drawn attention to complexities within the ecological communities we’re trying to recreate.

Charlotte’s results on this project are forthcoming, but to satiate your hunger for seeds, reintroduced mammals and what these mean for our landscapes, you can see some of Charlotte’s published work here and here.

Simple study question: What impact do herbivores have on vegetation communities?

Simple study answer: Different animals eat different things and in varying amounts!

Importance: Vital for understanding how our ecological communities work and how we can effectively ‘rewild’ modified landscapes.

In a word: Communities.

Read more about Charlotte’s research on her website here.

entry.title: Counting Cats Off Familiar Tracks
entry.content:
Sometimes we can be completely oblivious to places just off our usual tracks.

Australia is such a particularly vast continent that it can be somewhat awe-inspiring to consider how much of the country most Australians have never set foot in. Living in one of the smaller states, Victoria, I tend to assume I’ve pretty much seen it all.

So, it was refreshing to have the chance to go on a little exploratory adventure within my own state, in the coastal Glenelg region right on the border of Victoria and South Australia. This is one of those gorgeous places where patches of bush extend to the coastline, and while it’s relatively close to my usual haunts, the area was completely new to me.

Just as Glenelg has been hiding just off my tracks for years, the movements and habits of feral cats in Victoria have been similarly elusive. The impact feral cats have on Australian wildlife is well documented and undeniable, but the situation in Victoria remains somewhat mysterious.

[caption id="attachment_271" align="aligncenter" width="3264"] Some shifty looking feral cats caught mid-meal on camera. Images: Zoï Banikos, Matt Rees.[/caption]

This is partly due to feral cats not being classified as a pest in Victoria (yet), despite recommendations to do so in the Feral Cat Threat Abatement Plan, and the Northern Territory, Queensland, and South Australia already classifying them in this way. This technicality dramatically restricts the work researchers can do, preventing any trapping or radio-tracking of cats to establish densities or home ranges. Trapping cats can be near impossible anywhere, but if a researcher happens to catch one in Victoria they’re obliged to take it straight to a vet or animal shelter, just as you would with a domestic cat.

Another complication is that much of the Australian landscape is currently baited for foxes, and there’s evidence that foxes in turn control cats. So, it may be possible that fox baiting is actually further boosting feral cat numbers in Victoria...

Such a murky situation has led Matt Rees, a PhD candidate at the University of Melbourne with a questionable appetite for cats and caffeine, to embark on a project aiming to investigate cat numbers in these areas. Matt hopes to not only look at cat numbers but to investigate the relationship between cats and foxes. For example, cats may live in different areas to foxes, or they might only be active at times of day when foxes aren’t around.

After arriving from Queensland and being told his grand plans for cat trapping were impossible with the Victorian legislation, Matt has moved to using camera traps for the field component of his research.

Camera traps are just what they sound like – cameras where photos are triggered using motion or infrared sensors – and they are both a researcher’s blessing and curse. They allow for relatively non-invasive data collection from a distance, and over a long period of time. However, it can take many many hours to process the resulting footage. To increase the chances of the target species being seen by the cameras, lures, such as peanut butter baits for mammals, can be used to attract the target species.

So after a day of driving, Matt, myself, and another keen volunteer arrived at our home for the week and started constructing cat lures. This procedure involved us ripping up a horde of oil absorbing material (usually used by mechanics #reviewforscience) chucking it in a bucket and backing the hell away. Then Matt (because after all, it is his project) stirred the material in a wealth of tuna oil until it was soaked through and sufficiently pungent enough to attract a subsequent wealth of cats.

[caption id="attachment_272" align="alignnone" width="3264"] Matt demonstrating a more traditional use of the feather boa, and volunteer Steph preparing the cat lures. Images: Matt Rees.[/caption]

Donning gloves, we then embarked on the decidedly finicky job of fitting these stinking scraps of material into bait traps, which we then lovingly decorated with chopped up feather boas. (Non-ecologists should know this strange mix of craft and DIY is pretty standard in science).

Once we had each cat lure looking as delicately attractive as a cat lure with a feather boa can, we cooked up the traditional pre-fieldwork storm and Matt laid out a laminated map of his camera trap sites, perfectly arranged in a grid formation across the forest.

The cameras were split between two broad areas: areas baited for foxes, and areas without baiting. So, by recording cats and determining their density in these areas, Matt can figure out whether foxes are having an impact on cats – by changing their behaviour or habitat use – and therefore whether fox baiting may actually be heightening cat numbers. Matt is repeating this across other forests in Victoria, to see if he can find any consistent patterns.

So the next day we were out in the forest, attempting to get as close as possible to those points marked on Matt's map. Often fieldwork like this involves long treks with backpacks stashed with cameras, steep terrain and bush-bashing through potentially snake-ridden shoulder-high grass. We had it relatively easy in comparison because we were working in the beautifully flat and accessible Annya State Forest. Apart from one area with swampy terrain and grass towering above our heads, the GPS points tended to lie only a few easy hundred metres off the tracks.

[caption id="attachment_277" align="alignnone" width="3264"] Some of the critters we found: a confused koala, some kind of outstanding platyhelminthes (anyone?), one of many spiders on it's self-made mansion, and some abandoned emu eggs... Images: Matt Rees.[/caption]

Because of this, the fieldwork was mainly bushwalking through gorgeous Eucalypt forest, allowing us to spot a few cool critters on the way. The most recurring were the spiders, including a variety of colourful and spiny species which were surprisingly difficult to spot until you had pretty much destroyed their meticulous web work.

Eventually we would reach a set GPS point (or get as close as the terrain would allow) and start looking around for the perfect tree to mount the camera on. Once the camera was done we set up a cat lure and cleared the vegetation around it to prevent the camera trapping nightmare that is endless video footage of grass waving in the wind.

[caption id="attachment_273" align="alignnone" width="3264"] The ideal camera trap set-up: a clear space (with orchids untouched), one of our specially prepared cat lures, and, of course, the camera. Images: Matt Rees.[/caption]

Once we had checked (and double checked) the camera set-up was perfect, we trudged back through the forest, keeping our eyes peeled for spider webs. Unfortunately we usually failed at the latter, and were often still peeling remnant spider silk off our jackets once we were back in the car. Given a few months, Matt would be back with another car of keen volunteers, heading back into the forest to retrieve all the cameras.

From there, it’s on to processing the camera trap images, counting cats, and teasing out  how each individual moves around in their environment. Matt's endless number of photographs will unearth answers to our questions around feral cats in this forested environment, informing future management of cats and foxes, and further uncovering the mystery of feral cats in Victoria.

Study question: How many cats are out there, and does fox control actually benefit feral cats?

Importance: This work will inform future management of feral cats, and potentially foxes, in Victorian forests and similar environments across Australia.

In a word (almost): Forest ferals!

Read more about Matt’s research on his blog here.

entry.content:
I recently* attended a particularly academic dinner party, at which each guest was invited to present a five-minute talk on absolutely anything.

The topics covered were satisfyingly representative of my exceptional friends and their own passions and interests. We moved from a discussion of how cheap fast fashion reinforces capitalism, to why elves are essentially responsible for every fictional universe's issues, to what exactly my mate does for a living.

Unsurprisingly, I planned to talk about animals. And while I spent a while considering researching how a real fire-breathing dragon could actually exist (it would have been a real crowd pleaser), in the end I decided I respected real dragons too much to focus on a fictional animal.

Instead, I put together a slide show including both fictional and real fantastic creatures, which had the delightful effect of confusing the hell out of my friends.

I'll save you the tricks in this blog post and only present the animals that are categorically-certainly-absolutely-almost-definitely real, I promise. (Or are they?...)

Shield Shrimp (Triops australiensis)

[caption id="attachment_229" align="alignnone" width="1663"] Image: Internet Archive Book Images/Flickr[/caption]

This prehistoric creature has pretty much looked the same since the Triassic period. That's over 199 million years ago, when dinosaurs were still around...if that doesn't completely blow your mind then get out (or keep reading - something else might interest your twisted mind).

The Shield Shrimp can grow to around the size of a fist and has 60 legs which it breathes through, because who needs lungs? It appears in muddy puddles after rain in the arid lands of Australia, and causes excitement in (already excitable) ecology interns for weeks following...

Green-banded Broodsac (Leucochloridium paradoxum)

 

[caption id="attachment_246" align="alignnone" width="2032"] Image: Baudon/Wikimedia[/caption]

These parasitic flatworms use snails as their intermediate host in order to get at their definitive host: birds.

The flatworm infects snail's eye stalks so they move and flash like a caterpillar flashing their hazard lights, which turns out to be a great way to attract birds. The worm even manages to control the snail's mind and drive it into open areas, just in case a hungry bird couldn't spot the disco ball in the undergrowth.

The result is a happily ingested flatworm, a very screwed over (and eaten) snail, and a now infected bird. And so the (beautiful) life cycle continues.

Arctic Tern (Sterna paradisaea)

[caption id="attachment_248" align="alignnone" width="1284"] Image: Internet Archive Book Image/Flickr[/caption]

This magnificent bird circumnavigates the globe, undertaking the longest known migration of any animal in the world. It can travel a total of 2.4 million kilometres over its lifetime!

A virtually new fledgling can fly from London to Melbourne (over 22,000 km!) within a couple of months, and the species also flies from Canada to South Africa. That sure puts my marathon aspirations to shame.

Trilling Frog (Neobatrachus centralis)

[caption id="attachment_257" align="aligncenter" width="851"] Image**: Internet Archive Book Images/Flickr[/caption]

Like Shield Shrimp, these incredible amphibians emerge from underground after rainfall in arid regions. In some areas, these creatures are the most abundant vertebrate; the most common animal with a back-bone. Yet you can't see them!

Because they're hiding underground in torpor. Lying in wait...

Peacock Mantis Shrimp (Odontodactylus scyllarus)

[caption id="attachment_249" align="aligncenter" width="841"] Image: Biodiversity Heritage Library/Flickr[/caption]

This tiny crustacean has the fastest punch in the world. Its limb moves like an explosive latch or spring and the resulting force is 10,000 times the force of gravity!

The shrimp's punch is so fast it lowers the water pressure in front of them causing it to boil and emit light. (No big deal).

An electrotrophic bacterium (Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans)

Now here's a species which is pretty much a sci-fi alien come to life. So insane that no picture can really do it justice.

This bacterium feeds on electricity. That's right. Now pull your jaw off the floor and read on.

They feed on electrons which, to be fair, we all ultimately feed on through the magical process of cellular respiration in the powerhouses of our cells: the mitochondria. Surprise!

The difference is that we get our electrons from our food through glucose molecules. This bacterium usually uses Fe2+ ions as its electron source instead, but when these are not available the species has another option.

It is capable of sourcing its ions directly from an electrode, or in other words, directly from an electrical current! A species feeding on electricity, just wow...what's next evolution?

Gastric-brooding Frog (Rheobatrachus genus)

[caption id="attachment_256" align="alignright" width="298"] Image: Kelsey McGilvrey[/caption]

Like something out of the original fairytales, this frog (or rather, its genus) is famous for the females brooding young in their stomachs.

Once the eggs are fertilised the mother swallows them and the tadpoles hatch inside her stomach, only emerging once morphed into tiny froglets. Seriously. You can't make this stuff up.

The sad part? They're extinct; no individual has been sighted since 1981.

The species most likely went extinct due to chytrid fungus: a pathogen greatly threatening frogs worldwide to this day, and a pathogen humans are responsible for spreading.

All the animals above are truly fantastical and, in my humble (and biased) opinion, truly worth preserving. This is one of the reasons why both "basic" and applied research are so important.

One to find the wonder, and one to keep it.

Thanks to my lab mates Holly and Katie for suggesting some of these fantastic beasts!

*was recent when I first drafted this post...

**This image is not a drawing of the Trilling Frog. I apologise for this, but also feel fairly confident that 2 weeks of searching for one frog sketch is enough...

entry.title: How to Train a Bilby
entry.content:
I was nearing the end of a research internship in the arid zone, and keen for an excuse to keep clinging on to the red sand, when a rare opportunity appeared. A chance to get up close to one of Australia’s most curious looking species: the Greater Bilby.

I had caught many glimpses of bilbies while spotlighting and processing camera trap images during my internship, but I hadn’t had the chance to experience them up close.

Needless to say, I jumped at the opportunity.

[caption id="attachment_238" align="alignnone" width="1920"] A Greater Bilby (Macrotis lagotis): cause for celebration when trawling through endless camera trap pictures of waving grass. Image: Arid Recovery.[/caption]

The bilbies in question were hiding out within the Arid Recovery reserve in South Australia. This reserve encompasses 123 km2 of arid habitat, with around half of that being completely feral-free, meaning no foxes, rabbits, or cats. The rest of the reserve is split into two expansions with low densities of cats and rabbits. These expansions provide researchers with opportunities for experimentation, allowing for comparisons between the expansions and outside the fence.

The Greater Bilby, alongside a vast number of our native species, is threatened by feral cats and red foxes. Being a predator-free reserve, much of Arid Recovery’s research focuses on managing this threat.

And while feral cat control is crucial to prevent current impacts on our native species, it is unlikely we will ever be able to completely eradicate feral cats from the Australian landscape. Currently, native species struggle not only from the sheer density of cats but also because some species, particularly populations kept long-term in feral-free reserves, are naïve to the predators. They simply don’t recognise, or are not quick enough to recognise, the threat the cats pose to them.

[caption id="attachment_243" align="alignnone" width="4608"] Some feral cats become experts at hunting native animals within their territory. This is a Sand Goanna (Varanus gouldii) claw found in the stomach of a feral cat.[/caption]

There’s some chance populations will eventually learn to avoid this (relatively new) predator. Indeed, some species, such as Australian black snakes, have evolved to avoid eating the poisonous cane toad since it moved through their territory. However, such species still suffered major declines when the toad first arrived, and many of our native mammals, like the bilby, are already threatened by other factors (such as habitat restriction). The sheer density of cats is probably enough to push them towards extinction faster than they can evolve to face the threat. So, what can we do to help them along?

How about training them ourselves?

If we expose bilbies to low densities of cats, enough to give them experience with the predator, but not enough to substantially lower their population, could we kickstart the evolutionary process, and give bilbies a better chance outside predator free reserves? Previous research on Burrowing Bettongs (an insane species you've never heard of) suggests we can, but perhaps bilbies will react differently.

Enter PhD student Alexandra Ross (hereafter known as Aly).

Aly's project involves comparing the predator aversion of bilbies from two different populations within the Arid Recovery reserve, one exposed to cats (at a low density) and one not. The hope is that bilbies which have been exposed to cats should have greater predator aversion and therefore greater survival rates once rereleased.

To test this predator aversion, Aly had to observe in the field how long individual bilbies took to emerge from a burrow within a controlled pen. But to do this she needed to catch some first.

The trouble is bilbies are not trap-happy. Unlike bettongs who will stop at nothing to get their hands on a peanut bait, bilbies are much more cautious and so it is practically impossible to survey them by setting out traps. Instead, you must catch them by hand while spotlighting at night.

Aly therefore required bilby chasers, and I was one of them. Our job was to jump out of a 4WD as quickly as possible, sprint our guts out towards a bilby, and manage to catch it safely in a soft felt capture bag. We would then take the bilby to a pen where Aly could conduct behavioural trials to test their predator aversion tactics, before taking them safely back to their capture point before dawn.

Setting out well after dark, we started driving within the reserve, three of us with our arms out the windows waving spotlights back and forth and back and forth. Our eyes searching and scanning and hoping for bilbies, and the moment one appeared…

'STOP! BILBY!'

Hands on door handles, us three volunteers in the back readied ourselves.

Aly slammed on the brakes and pulled the 4WD to a stop, yelling 'GO GO GO!’. The moment the car halted we threw ourselves outside of it.

Nets in hand, we ran, we sprinted, we almost tore our muscles apart soaring out into the darkness. Adrenaline and instinct drove us on, the first 30 seconds of running we were barely conscious for determination.

The light from our head torches was shining out onto the dirt, sand, and rocks. The edge of our lights caught the flick of a white fluffy tail and we geared towards it, yelling encouragement to each other as we went.

Each time we tried to take some kind of strategic formation, one in the middle and one either side to cut the bilby off. Sometimes it worked. Normally it didn't. The bilby was too fast, too agile, or disappeared down into a burrow.

If there was a sand dune we tried to cut them off from it. Once on the dunes we had no chance against the bilbies, they danced up the sand with no effort at all, while we slogged up as if our legs are already knee-deep in quicksand.

We were at our best on the swales: the flats in between sand dunes. Ideally the ground would be just dirt or low grass, but occasionally we would be running across rocky gibber plains, dreading a wrong step and an ankle-twisting landing.

It was a lucky break whenever we spotted a bilby close to the road. My first catch was right outside my door when I spotted him but he had deftly darted away by the time we humans were outside the car.

But I ran like absolute hell, not daring to take my eyes away from that tuft of white fur for a moment. We all ran out into the darkness, leaping over bushes and hoping against wild hope that we would eventually wear him out.

Thankfully he ran into a collection of bushes and I and another volunteer were soon onto him and gently placing him into a felt capture bag. Success!

[caption id="attachment_143" align="aligncenter" width="455"] A Greater Bilby (Macrotis lagotis), and myself. I decided this animal was my spirit animal when I was in year 2. Coincidence? (Probably.) Image: Aly Ross.[/caption]

Each captured bilby was kept for the least amount of time as possible to minimise stress, and released in the exact location they were picked up with plenty of time for them to forage and return to their burrow before sun up.

Work like this is essential for threatened species conservation; effectively monitoring individuals and populations is critical to understanding how animals are going and how best to manage their ongoing survival.

Around half a century ago, we lost the Lesser Bilby to extinction. This time around we have so many hard-working land managers, researchers and volunteers trying to save the Greater Bilby. So this Easter (and the next) consider celebrating bilbies (not bunnies) to support their work.

The Greater Bilby is a bizarre, marvellous, and utterly unique Australian species, and it would be a mighty shame to lose it.

Simple study question: Can exposure to cats provide bilbies with the survival skills to live alongside feral cat populations?

Simple study answer: We’ll soon find out! (Research in progress.)

Importance: This work may provide a way to train up our native species to survive despite burgeoning cat populations.

In a word: Training

The rest of the reserve is split into two expansions with low densities of cats and rabbits. These expansions provide researchers with opportunities for experimentation, allowing for comparisons between the expansions and outside the fence. The Greater Bilby, alongside a vast number of our native species, is threatened by feral cats and red foxes. Being a predator-free reserve, much of Arid Recovery’s research focuses on managing this threat. And while feral cat control is crucial to prevent current impacts on our native species, it is unlikely we will ever be able to completely eradicate feral cats from the Australian landscape. Currently, native species struggle not only from the sheer density of cats but also because some species, particularly populations kept long-term in feral-free reserves, are naïve to the predators. They simply don’t recognise, or are not quick enough to recognise, the threat the cats pose to them. [caption id="attachment_243" align="alignnone" width="4608"] Some feral cats become experts at hunting native animals within their territory. This is a Sand Goanna (Varanus gouldii) claw found in the stomach of a feral cat.[/caption] There’s some chance populations will eventually learn to avoid this (relatively new) predator. Indeed, some species, such as Australian black snakes, have evolved to avoid eating the poisonous cane toad since it moved through their territory. However, such species still suffered major declines when the toad first arrived, and many of our native mammals, like the bilby, are already threatened by other factors (such as habitat restriction). The sheer density of cats is probably enough to push them towards extinction faster than they can evolve to face the threat. So, what can we do to help them along? How about training them ourselves? If we expose bilbies to low densities of cats, enough to give them experience with the predator, but not enough to substantially lower their population, could we kickstart the evolutionary process, and give bilbies a better chance outside predator free reserves? Previous research on Burrowing Bettongs (an insane species you've never heard of) suggests we can, but perhaps bilbies will react differently. Enter PhD student Alexandra Ross (hereafter known as Aly). Aly's project involves comparing the predator aversion of bilbies from two different populations within the Arid Recovery reserve, one exposed to cats (at a low density) and one not. The hope is that bilbies which have been exposed to cats should have greater predator aversion and therefore greater survival rates once rereleased. To test this predator aversion, Aly had to observe in the field how long individual bilbies took to emerge from a burrow within a controlled pen. But to do this she needed to catch some first. The trouble is bilbies are not trap-happy. Unlike bettongs who will stop at nothing to get their hands on a peanut bait, bilbies are much more cautious and so it is practically impossible to survey them by setting out traps. Instead, you must catch them by hand while spotlighting at night. Aly therefore required bilby chasers, and I was one of them. Our job was to jump out of a 4WD as quickly as possible, sprint our guts out towards a bilby, and manage to catch it safely in a soft felt capture bag. We would then take the bilby to a pen where Aly could conduct behavioural trials to test their predator aversion tactics, before taking them safely back to their capture point before dawn. Setting out well after dark, we started driving within the reserve, three of us with our arms out the windows waving spotlights back and forth and back and forth. Our eyes searching and scanning and hoping for bilbies, and the moment one appeared… 'STOP! BILBY!' Hands on door handles, us three volunteers in the back readied ourselves. Aly slammed on the brakes and pulled the 4WD to a stop, yelling 'GO GO GO!’. The moment the car halted we threw ourselves outside of it. Nets in hand, we ran, we sprinted, we almost tore our muscles apart soaring out into the darkness. Adrenaline and instinct drove us on, the first 30 seconds of running we were barely conscious for determination. The light from our head torches was shining out onto the dirt, sand, and rocks. The edge of our lights caught the flick of a white fluffy tail and we geared towards it, yelling encouragement to each other as we went. Each time we tried to take some kind of strategic formation, one in the middle and one either side to cut the bilby off. Sometimes it worked. Normally it didn't. The bilby was too fast, too agile, or disappeared down into a burrow. If there was a sand dune we tried to cut them off from it. Once on the dunes we had no chance against the bilbies, they danced up the sand with no effort at all, while we slogged up as if our legs are already knee-deep in quicksand. We were at our best on the swales: the flats in between sand dunes. Ideally the ground would be just dirt or low grass, but occasionally we would be running across rocky gibber plains, dreading a wrong step and an ankle-twisting landing. It was a lucky break whenever we spotted a bilby close to the road. My first catch was right outside my door when I spotted him but he had deftly darted away by the time we humans were outside the car. But I ran like absolute hell, not daring to take my eyes away from that tuft of white fur for a moment. We all ran out into the darkness, leaping over bushes and hoping against wild hope that we would eventually wear him out. Thankfully he ran into a collection of bushes and I and another volunteer were soon onto him and gently placing him into a felt capture bag. Success! [caption id="attachment_143" align="aligncenter" width="455"] A Greater Bilby (Macrotis lagotis), and myself. I decided this animal was my spirit animal when I was in year 2. Coincidence? (Probably.) Image: Aly Ross.[/caption] Each captured bilby was kept for the least amount of time as possible to minimise stress, and released in the exact location they were picked up with plenty of time for them to forage and return to their burrow before sun up. Work like this is essential for threatened species conservation; effectively monitoring individuals and populations is critical to understanding how animals are going and how best to manage their ongoing survival. Around half a century ago, we lost the Lesser Bilby to extinction. This time around we have so many hard-working land managers, researchers and volunteers trying to save the Greater Bilby. So this Easter (and the next) consider celebrating bilbies (not bunnies) to support their work. The Greater Bilby is a bizarre, marvellous, and utterly unique Australian species, and it would be a mighty shame to lose it. Simple study question: Can exposure to cats provide bilbies with the survival skills to live alongside feral cat populations? Simple study answer: We’ll soon find out! (Research in progress.) Importance: This work may provide a way to train up our native species to survive despite burgeoning cat populations. In a word: Training

entry.title: Internship at Arid Recovery
entry.content:
I'm hoping to start on some posts for this blog in the near future, but in the meantime I would love to share some photos and experiences from my internship at Arid Recovery in the first half of 2017.

Arid Recovery is an independent, not-for-profit conservation initiative which has been working just outside Roxby Downs since 1997. The reserve incorporates 123 km² of fenced reserve with about half being feral-free (i.e. free of cats, foxes, and rabbits). The reserve has successfully reintroduced populations of the Burrowing Bettong, Greater Stick-nest rat, Western Barred Bandicoot, and Greater Bilby. Plains mice and Spinifex Hopping Mice have also reintroduced themselves (!) reaching astounding numbers.

[caption id="attachment_media-66" align="alignnone" width="3996"] The Big 4 at Arid Recovery: (L-R) the Greater Stick-nest Rat, Burrowing Bettong, Greater Bilby, and Western Barred Bandicoot, shown through camera trap images. Photos: Arid Recovery[/caption]

My fellow intern Nathan Beerkens (now Field Ecologist & Community Coordinator!), wrote a stellar post describing A Day in the Life of an Arid Recovery intern, which will give you a good idea of what kind of work we were doing day-to-day. Basically lots of camera trap checks, community engagement, and work on individual projects, which for me involved even more camera trap footage and staking out some rabbit warrens outside the reserve fence.

We were also lucky enough to help out during the annual pitfall trapping, which was a massive highlight for me, as a reptile-lover with little hands-on experience until that point. I wrote a post on that incredible week on Arid Recovery's blog which you can find here.

[caption id="attachment_16" align="alignnone" width="2048"] Some seriously charismatic reptile species on the Arid Recovery reserve: (L-R) Bearded Dragon, Sand Goanna, Fat-tailed Gecko)[/caption]

Many late nights were spent spotlighting both within and outside the reserve, often with the wonderful Hugh McGregor. This occasionally included playing around with a thermal camera I became increasingly obsessed with. Another particularly valuable experience for me was running group tours to the reserve, which incorporated such taxing work as watching sunsets, drawing attention to exciting tracks and nests, and spotlighting for the Big 4 (as pictured in the camera traps above).

My obsession with the arid environment was fully cemented by the tracks in the sand.  What appears to be a relatively desolate landscape suddenly seems near to bursting when you realise the ground is covered by signs of life. The excitement that comes from identifying tracks cannot be understated, and it was particularly thrilling to come across bilby tracks! (Although I also find sleepy / stumpy-tail / shingleback lizard tracks to be pretty spectacular).

[caption id="attachment_media-37" align="alignnone" width="3996"] Tracks within the landscape at Arid Recovery: (L-R) Burrowing Bettong tracks, Shingleback/Sleepy/Stumpy-tail Lizard tracks, mess of tracks including Plains and Hopping Mice[/caption]

Nearing the end of the internship, my semi-severe peanut allergy unfortunately counted me out of annual bettong trapping (but see a blog and video about it here). However, the extraordinarily awesome silver lining was that I ended up catching bilbies instead! It was so incredible to see these marvellous creatures up close, and a wonderful experience to bring the internship to a close.

Since leaving I've already returned to volunteer on some vegetation surveys, and I plan to return for pitfall trapping this year if I can. It goes without saying that I recommend you take a visit to catch a glimpse of the "Big 4" (stickies, bettongs, bilbies, and bandicoots). I also suggest, if possible, that you take a careful look both inside and outside the fence to see for yourself the striking difference in the animal (in the tracks) and plant communities, resulting from feral predator exclusion.

I would like to thank all the staff at Arid Recovery, particularly Kath, Kim, John, Hugh, and Nathan for such a wonderful experience and a great time!
